wiki_excerpt:
The Colt M1911 (also known as 1911, Colt 1911, Colt .45, or Colt Government in the case of Colt-produced models) is a single-action, recoil-operated, semi-automatic pistol chambered primarily for the .45 ACP cartridge.


History


Early history and adaptations
The M1911 pistol originated in the late 1890s as the result of a search for a suitable self-loading (or semi-automatic) pistol to replace the variety of revolvers in service at the time. The United States was rapidly adopting new firearms; several new pistols and two all-new service rifles (M1892/96/98 Krag and M1895 Navy Lee), as well as a series of revolvers by Colt and Smith & Wesson for the Army and Navy, were adopted within this decade. The revolvers were becoming more reliable then but did not have the firepower needed to be as effective as the M1911.
The next decade saw a similar pace, adopting several more revolvers; an intensive search for a self-loading pistol eventually led to the adoption of the M1911 after the turn of the decade. Hiram S. Maxim had designed a self-loading rifle in the 1880s, but was preoccupied with machine guns. Nevertheless, the application of his recoil-energy reloading principle led to several self-loading pistols in 1896. The designs caught the attention of various militaries, each of which began programs to find a suitable one for their forces. In the U.S., such a program would lead to a formal test at the turn of the 20th century.

During the end of 1899 and into 1900, a test of self-loading pistols was conducted, including entries from Mauser (C96 "Broomhandle"), Mannlicher (Mannlicher M1894), and Colt (Colt M1900). This led to a purchase of 1,000 DWM Luger pistols, chambered in 7.65mm Luger. During field trials, these ran into some problems, especially with stopping power. Other governments had made similar complaints. Consequently, DWM produced an enlarged version of the round, the 9×19mm Parabellum, with fifty weapons chambered for it, tested by the U.S. Army in 1903.
American units fighting Tausūg guerrillas in the Moro Rebellion in Sulu during the Philippine–American War using the then-standard Colt M1892 revolver, .38 Long Colt, found it to be unsuitable for the rigors of jungle warfare, particularly in terms of stopping power, as the Moros had high battle morale and often used drugs to inhibit the sensation of pain.
The U.S. Army briefly reverted to using the M1873 single-action revolver in .45 Colt caliber, which had been standard during the late 19th century; the heavier bullet was found to be more effective against charging tribesmen. Problems prompted General William Crozier, the Chief of Ordnance, to authorize further testing for a new service pistol.

grok_lead: The M1911 is a single-action, semi-automatic, recoil-operated pistol chambered for the.45 ACP cartridge, designed by American firearms inventor John Moses Browning. Featuring a 5-inch barrel, it employs a short-recoil locking system with a tilting barrel and holds seven rounds in a detachable single-stack box magazine. Selected by the U.S. Army after rigorous pistol trials conducted from 1906 to 1911 to address the limitations of.38-caliber revolvers in stopping power, the Colt-submitted Browning design was officially adopted on March 29, 1911, as the standard-issue sidearm for U.S. forces, marking the first semi-automatic pistol to enter widespread military service. The pistol's robust construction, manual thumb safety, and grip safety contributed to its reputation for reliability under adverse conditions, enabling effective close-quarters combat. Serving continuously from World War I through World War II, the Korean War, and the Vietnam Warâspanning over seven decades of primary or secondary useâthe M1911 demonstrated exceptional durability and the.45 ACP round's superior man-stopping capability compared to smaller calibers. An updated M1911A1 variant, incorporating ergonomic improvements like a shorter trigger and arched mainspring housing, was standardized in 1924 and produced in large numbers during World War II. Though formally replaced by the 9mm Beretta M9 in 1985, the M1911's design principles continue to influence modern handguns and remain favored by special operations units for their proven performance.
